planting.note: Set bare-root crowns or potted rhizomes once soil has warmed, training bines up twine or a trellis as soon as shoots emerge.

directions: A low-alpha noble-type aroma hop bred from German Hallertau stock at Oregon State, prized by home brewers for clean, mild spicy-herbal character in pilsners and lagers. Give it deep, well-drained, fertile soil and a sturdy 12-18 foot support, since bines climb aggressively once established. Cut the first-year crown back hard after frost and mulch heavily to protect the root system through winter. Expect only a token harvest the first year, with full cone production arriving by year three.

planting.note: Plant crowns in a sunny, sheltered spot with rich loam, since this heirloom English cultivar is more disease-prone than modern American hops.

directions: One of the oldest named English hop varieties, treasured for its delicate honeyed, earthy-floral aroma that defines classic English bitters and pale ales. It is somewhat lower-yielding and more susceptible to verticillium wilt and downy mildew than newer cultivars, so give it good air circulation and avoid overhead watering. Home growers in cooler, humid climates similar to Kent, England tend to have the best luck. Harvest cones when they feel dry and papery and spring back after a gentle squeeze.

planting.note: Give this classic German landrace deep, humus-rich soil and full sun, and expect it to need more attention to disease pressure than American-bred cultivars.

directions: The archetypal noble aroma hop, mild and spicy-herbal, that defines authentic German lagers and pilsners. It is a low-yielding, slow-to-establish landrace variety that is genetically susceptible to Verticillium wilt, so home growers should source certified disease-free rhizomes and rotate planting sites if problems appear. Full sun and steady moisture during the summer bine-growth push are essential for reasonable cone set. Because true Hallertau is finicky, many home brewers substitute Mount Hood or Liberty, but growing the genuine article is a rewarding project for patient gardeners.
sources: Bavarian State Research Center for Agriculture (LfL)

planting.note: Provide a tall trellis and consistent moisture; this German noble variety is closely related to Saaz and shares its mild, refined aroma.

directions: A traditional Bavarian noble hop from the Tettnang region, related to Saaz and used for its subtle, spicy-floral aroma in lagers, pilsners, and Belgian-style ales. Like other noble varieties it yields modestly compared to American hops and appreciates deep, fertile soil with good drainage to reduce root disease risk. Train bines clockwise up strings each spring and remove the weakest shoots to focus energy into two or three strong bines per crown. Harvest when cones are dry, springy, and lupulin-rich at the base of the petals.

planting.note: A vigorous, disease-resistant English cultivar that tolerates a wider range of home-garden conditions than the finicky noble hops.

directions: A reliable dual-purpose hop with woodsy, minty-resinous character, popular for California common (steam) beer, brown ales, and smoked beers. It is notably vigorous and more tolerant of cool, damp climates and less-than-ideal soil than many aroma cultivars, making it a forgiving choice for first-time hop growers. Give it a sturdy 15-20 foot support since mature bines produce heavy cone loads. Side-dress with compost each spring and watch for aphids, which this variety attracts more than most.

planting.note: One of the highest-yielding bittering hops for the home garden; give it maximum sun and a tall, sturdy trellis.

directions: A high-alpha American bittering hop bred at USDA-Idaho, valued by home brewers for heavy, reliable cone production and clean grapefruit-citrus bittering character. It stores well and resists many common hop diseases better than older bittering varieties, making it a low-maintenance choice. Provide rich, well-drained soil, full sun, and generous vertical space, since Galena regularly produces the heaviest cone yields of any widely grown home-garden hop. Harvest promptly once cones dry and papery to preserve alpha acid content.

planting.note: A New Zealand-bred cultivar with distinctive white-wine-grape aroma; give it full sun and consistent moisture through the growing season.

directions: Named for its uncanny resemblance to Sauvignon Blanc wine grapes, this New Zealand hop delivers intense tropical fruit, gooseberry, and white-wine aromatics that home brewers use heavily in New Zealand and West Coast IPAs. It performs best in mild, maritime-influenced climates and appreciates protection from intense midday heat in hot inland regions. Provide a tall trellis, rich soil, and consistent irrigation, since inconsistent moisture noticeably dulls its signature aroma. Pick cones promptly at peak ripeness, as its delicate aromatics fade quickly if harvest is delayed.

planting.note: Transplant into a large container or shaded understory spot once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 60F.

directions: A natural giant-leaved mutation discovered in Brazil, grown by home coffee enthusiasts mainly as a novelty for its unusually large leaves, cherries, and beans, which are roughly double the size of standard Arabica. It is lower-yielding and slower to bear than compact modern cultivars, so patience is required before the first harvest. Grow in bright, dappled shade with rich, acidic, well-drained potting mix, and protect from any temperature below 50F. Its dramatic size makes it a popular specimen plant in home greenhouses and sunrooms even where fruit production is modest.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: This vigorous, taller-growing Arabica benefits from extra headroom if grown in a greenhouse or large container.

directions: A natural Brazilian hybrid of Typica and Bourbon discovered in the 1940s, valued for combining a robust, disease-tolerant constitution with excellent cup quality. It grows noticeably larger and more vigorously than dwarf cultivars like Caturra, so home growers need generous container size or in-ground space with good headroom. Provide bright, filtered light, steady warmth above 60F, and rich, well-drained acidic soil, and expect a longer wait to first harvest than compact modern hybrids. Its vigor and disease tolerance make it one of the more forgiving Arabica types for home cultivation.

planting.note: Give this high-altitude selection cool nights and bright, filtered light for the best flavor development in home cultivation.

directions: A famous Typica-derived selection traditionally grown in Jamaica's cool, misty Blue Mountains, prized for a smooth, mild, low-acid cup with almost no bitterness. Home growers outside true high-elevation tropics won't replicate the legendary flavor exactly, but the plant itself performs well in bright, filtered light with rich, well-drained acidic soil and protection from hot, drying wind. It is slower-growing and lower-yielding than commercial hybrids, which suits its role as a specialty collector's plant rather than a high-volume producer. Keep humidity moderate to reduce fungal leaf disease, which this selection is somewhat prone to in humid lowland conditions.

planting.note: Transplant into deep shade with warm, humid, wind-protected conditions well after all danger of cool weather has passed.

directions: An heirloom Ecuadorian cacao renowned among chocolate makers for its distinctive floral, jasmine-like 'arriba' flavor note found in no other cacao type. It is more disease-susceptible and lower-yielding than modern hybrid clones, so home growers should prioritize excellent drainage, high humidity, and dappled shade under taller canopy trees or shade cloth to reduce stress. Keep young trees sheltered from wind and direct sun, and maintain consistently warm, humid conditions year-round since this variety has no cold tolerance whatsoever. Best suited to true tropical home gardens or heated greenhouse collections rather than casual container culture in temperate climates.
